prompt:
Power $P$ is defined as the rate of doing work: $P = \frac{W}{t}$, where work done $W$ is defined by $W = F d$ and force $F$ is defined by $F = m a$.
(a) State the SI base units of force. [1]
(b) Show that the SI base units of work are $\text{kg m}^2\text{ s}^{-2}$. [1]
(c) Hence, derive the SI base units of the watt ($\text{W}$). [1]

mark_scheme.criterion: (b) Shows multiplication by distance: (kg m s^-2) x m = kg m^2 s^-2.
(c) Shows division by time: (kg m^2 s^-2) / s = kg m^2 s^-3.

hints: In (a), force is mass times acceleration.
In (b), multiply force units by metres.
In (c), divide work units by seconds: subtract 1 from the power of s (-2 - 1 = -3).
solution:
(a) From F = ma, [F] = kg x m s^-2 = kg m s^-2.
(b) From W = Fd, [W] = [F] x [d] = (kg m s^-2) x m = kg m^2 s^-2.
(c) From P = W/t, [P] = [W] / [t] = (kg m^2 s^-2) / s = kg m^2 s^-3. Therefore, 1 W = 1 kg m^2 s^-3.
teacher_walkthrough: Three-step logical chain: force -> work -> power.

provenance.independence_statement: Authored as an original medium question deriving the base units of the watt.
